1.text:
The Qurʾān's longest chapter begins with three letters and no sentence. *Alif-Lãm-Mĩm* is not a word, and it does not say anything. That is not a mistake in the text, and it is not a piece missing from the beginning. The Qurʾān opens twenty-nine of its chapters this way, on purpose. Scholars have argued about what the letters mean for fourteen centuries and never agreed. The short answer is that their meaning belongs to Allah. What is clear is what they do: they put the raw material of the Qurʾān in front of you before the argument starts, and they make the point that you cannot build a book like this one out of them.

**What the letters are called.**

Maʿārif gives the term and the reason for it: each of these letters is pronounced separately, without a vowel sound added after it, which is why the technical name is *muqaṭṭaʿāt* — isolated or disconnected letters. Tazkīrul Qurʾān supplies the scale of the thing, and the scale matters, because it tells you this is a pattern and not a curiosity: the *muqaṭṭaʿāt* open twenty-nine chapters, in combinations such as *Alif Lām Mīm*, *Hā Mīm*, *Nūn*, *ʿAyn Sīn* and *Qāf*, and some of them became the names of the sūrahs themselves — *Ṭā Hā*, *Yā Sīn*, *Ṣād*, *Qāf*. So a reader meets this device again and again through the Book, and every time it does the same thing. It stops the reading before the reading has started.

**The readings on what they mean.**

Tanwīr al-Miqbās preserves the fullest list, transmitting from Ibn ʿAbbās: *Alif stands for Allah, Lām for the Archangel Gabriel, and Mīm for Muḥammad.* Then two further readings follow in the same breath — that the three letters stand for Allah's blessings, His kindness and His dominion; or that each is the opening letter of one of His names, *Allāh*, *al-Laṭīf* and *al-Majīd*. And then the reading that ends the list, and outlasted the others: *it is also said that only Allah knows the meaning of these disjointed letters, while some maintain that it is an oath that He made.* Four explanations in one paragraph, and the last is the one that held.

**Why the majority stopped there.**

Maʿārif records where the weight of opinion settled, and the reasoning is historical rather than clever. Some commentators held that the isolated letters are the names of the sūrahs they open; others that they are symbols of the Divine Names. But the majority of the Companions, of the Tābiʿīn after them, and of the later authoritative scholars preferred the view that they are symbols or mysteries whose meaning is known to Allah alone, or was entrusted to the Prophet ﷺ as a secret not to be passed on. The argument that decides it is the silence: no explanation of these letters was ever reported from him. Had he been given their meaning to convey, he would have conveyed it. Al-Qurṭubī adopted precisely this position. Al-Jalālayn compresses the entire question into five words — *God knows best what He means by these letters* — which is not an evasion but the conclusion the evidence supports.

**What the letters are doing instead.**

Because if their meaning is closed, their function is not, and Al-Mukhtaṣar states that function in a single move. The letters have no meaning in themselves, yet they have a purpose, and since there is divine wisdom in everything in the Qurʾān, they *point to the miracle of the Qurʾān, made up of the letters which make up the words we speak.* That is the challenge stripped to its shortest form. Here are three of your letters, unarranged and unexplained. The Book that follows is built from the same stock, and you cannot produce it. The letters are not a puzzle to be solved; they are the raw material laid on the table before the argument begins. Al-Mukhtaṣar adds the structural confirmation: sūrahs that begin with these letters are usually followed by a verse about the Qurʾān itself — which is exactly what verse 2 does.

**The sūrah they open.**

Ibn Kathīr's entry on this verse is not about the letters at all. It is titled the virtues of Sūrat al-Baqarah, and it collects what the sūrah is worth, which is a strange and fitting thing to find attached to three unexplained letters. Abū Hurayrah reports the Prophet ﷺ saying, *Do not turn your houses into graves. Verily, Shayṭān does not enter the house where Sūrat al-Baqarah is recited* — carried by Aḥmad, Muslim, at-Tirmidhī and an-Nasāʾī, and graded ḥasan ṣaḥīḥ. ʿAbdullāh ibn Masʿūd put it more bluntly: Shayṭān flees from the house where al-Baqarah is heard, and ad-Dārīmī preserves his version in which he flees passing wind. The same source gives the practical form: ten āyāt of al-Baqarah recited in a night keep Shayṭān out of the house — four from the beginning, Āyat al-Kursī, the two after it, and the last three. Saḥl ibn Saʿd reports that everything has a high peak and al-Baqarah is the high peak of the Qurʾān. And at-Tirmidhī records the expedition on which the Prophet ﷺ asked each man what he had memorised, came to the youngest, heard that he knew al-Baqarah, and made him commander over men older than himself. One of the notables objected that he had deliberately avoided learning it, for fear he could not implement it. That objection is the point of the sūrah, and of the three letters in front of it. The Book does not open with a summary of its contents. It opens with a demonstration that you cannot make one, and then asks whether you are going to obey it.

2.text:
The Qurʾān makes two flat claims about itself in this verse, and it makes them without argument. *This is the Book!* — and there is nothing doubtful about it. Then: it is *a guide*. But notice the second claim has a limit on it. It does not say the Book guides everyone. It says it guides those who are mindful of Allah. So the guidance is offered to all and received by some, and the rest of this chapter is largely about the difference between the two.

*This is the Book! There is no doubt about it* — a guide for those mindful ˹of Allah˺. The sūrah that opened with three unexplained letters now makes its first flat claim, and Maʿārif notices something in the grammar that most readers pass over. The Arabic says *dhālika al-kitāb*, using *dhālika*, the pronoun that points at something **far away**, to refer to a Book that is sitting right in front of the reader. That mismatch is deliberate. Maʿārif's reading is that the pronoun points backwards to the prayer at the end of al-Fātiḥah — *guide us to the straight path* — and announces that the request has been answered. The straight path you asked for is this.

**What "no doubt" is denying.**

Ibn Kathīr settles the word first: *rayb* means doubt, and he lists the chain that says so — Ibn ʿAbbās through as-Suddī, Ibn Masʿūd through Murrah al-Hamadānī, and a further roll of Abū ad-Dardāʾ, Mujāhid, Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, ʿAṭāʾ, Abū al-ʿĀliyah, ar-Rabīʿ ibn Anas, Muqātil ibn Ḥayyān, Qatādah and Ismāʿīl ibn Abī Khālid — closing with Ibn Abī Ḥātim's remark that *I do not know of any disagreement over this explanation.* Some took the sentence as a command rather than a statement: do not doubt it. Maʿārif then draws the distinction that makes the claim precise, because there are two ways a statement can be doubted. Either the statement itself is wrong, or the listener misunderstands a statement that is right. The verse closes both doors at once: there is nothing erroneous in the Book, and it is not obscure either.

**The two claims, in order.**

Al-Jalālayn gives the syntax that holds them together. The negation *lā rayba fīhi* is the predicate of *dhālika*, and the use of the distant demonstrative is there to glorify the Book. Then a second predicate follows — *hudā*, guidance — meaning the Book guides. So the verse asserts origin before effect: this is from God, therefore it guides. Tanwīr al-Miqbās puts the same sequence in the first person, as God speaking: *There is no doubt that it has come from Me; if you believe in it, I shall guide you, but if you do not believe in it, I will torment you.*

**Why the guidance is not automatic.**

The verse does not say the Book guides everyone, and Tazkīrul Qurʾān presses exactly there. There is no doubt that the Qurʾān is a book of guidance, but it guides only those who are sincere in their search for truth and anxious to be guided. The search is built into human nature; what is required is that a person uncover it. The vague yearnings of that nature then begin to receive a definite response, and the response is faith. So the guidance is real and unconditional in its offer, and conditional in its reception — the door is open, but you have to walk through it.

**Who the God-fearing are.**

The verse names its recipients as *al-muttaqīn*, and the sources gloss the word consistently. Al-Jalālayn: those who tend towards piety by adhering to what is commanded and avoiding what is prohibited, *thereby guarding themselves from the Fire.* Tanwīr al-Miqbās: those who ward off disbelief, associating partners with Allah, and indecencies. Al-Mukhtaṣar compresses it to a direction — the Book guides those mindful of Allah *to the way that leads to Him.* That is the promise the next two verses will describe in detail, by listing what such people actually do.

3.text:
These are the people the last verse was talking about, and they are described in three strokes. *They believe in the unseen* — things they cannot see or prove, like God, the angels, and the Day of Judgment. They *establish prayer* — not merely perform it, but keep it up. And they *donate from what We have provided for them* — they give money away. Belief, worship, and generosity. Nothing here is hidden or mystical, and nothing here can be done by feeling alone.

*Who believe in the unseen, establish prayer, and donate from what We have provided for them.* Three qualities, and Maʿārif explains why they come first. The two verses that follow the claim of guidance delineate the qualities of the God-fearing, and in doing so they contain *in essence a definition of faith* and an account of its basic tenets. So this is not a list of nice habits. It is the definition, given three ways: belief, worship, and money.

**What faith actually is.**

Ibn Kathīr opens on the word itself and lets the early authorities disagree productively. ʿAbdullāh ibn Masʿūd said *īmān* means to trust; az-Zuhrī said it is the deeds; ar-Rabīʿ ibn Anas said it means they fear Allah. Then at-Ṭabarī reconciles them, and his formulation is the one the tradition kept: the preferred view is that they are described as having faith in the unseen *by the tongue, deed and creed.* Faith is therefore a single reality with three instruments. Ibn Kathīr draws out what that means practically — a general term covering affirmation of Allah, His Books and His Messengers, *realised through adhering to the implications of what the tongue utters.* A creed that stops at the tongue is not yet īmān.

**Why the unseen comes first.**

Because it is the test. Al-Jalālayn glosses it as what is hidden from them — the Resurrection, Paradise and the Fire. Tanwīr al-Miqbās expands the list to Paradise, hell, the Bridge, the Scale, the Resurrection and the Reckoning, and then offers two further readings: that the unseen means whatever the Qurʾān reveals of what is not visible, and that the unseen is Allah Himself. Tazkīrul Qurʾān supplies the psychology, and it is the most useful thing said about this word anywhere in these sources. The urge to submit to some superior power later takes the form of bowing to the Almighty; the wish to sacrifice oneself for a greater good later takes the form of spending wealth for God's cause. Faith in the unseen is not one more item on a creed. It is the moment the vague yearning becomes a definite response.

**Establishing prayer.**

The word is *yuqīmūn*, they establish, not merely they perform. Tanwīr al-Miqbās reads it as completing the five prescribed prayers including the ablution before them, the bowing and prostrations within them, and the appointed timings that govern them. Every one of those is a discipline rather than a feeling, which is why the verse chose this verb.

**Spending.**

The third quality is money, and it is not an afterthought. Tanwīr al-Miqbās: of the wealth We have given them, they give charity — or, on another reading, they give the poor-due, zakāh, and the reference is to Abū Bakr and his companions. Al-Jalālayn keeps it general: they expend in obedience to God. Note the logic of the phrase the sources all preserve — *of what We have provided them.* The wealth is not theirs in the first place. They are distributing something they were given, which changes the act from generosity into returning a deposit.

**The shape of the definition.**

Three qualities, and they are not interchangeable. The first is inward and cannot be checked by anyone. The second is a repeated physical discipline with fixed times. The third is measurable, public, and costs something. Maʿārif's point is that a definition of faith built from those three excludes both the person who feels devout and does nothing, and the person who performs correctly and believes nothing. The unseen and the seen, There is a further reason the unseen is listed before prayer and spending, and it is that the other two qualities are visible. Anyone can observe a person praying or watch him give money away. Only belief in what cannot be seen is unverifiable from outside, which makes it the one quality that cannot be faked — and it is precisely the quality the hypocrites of verse 8 will counterfeit. The order is therefore diagnostic. The Qurʾān puts first the thing that will be hardest for the rest of the sūrah's third group to produce. The next verse adds a fourth quality, and then the fifth verse pronounces the verdict.

4.text:
A fourth quality, and it is about loyalty across time. *They believe in what has been revealed to you* — the Qurʾān — *and what was revealed before you* — the Torah, the Gospel, and the earlier scriptures. They do not pick and choose between the prophets. Then the verse ends on certainty: they have *sure faith in the Hereafter*. Not hope, not preference. Certainty about something they have not yet seen.

*And who believe in what has been revealed to you* ˹O Prophet˺ *and what was revealed before you, and have sure faith in the Hereafter.* The fourth quality is continuity, and Ibn Kathīr states it as a refusal to pick and choose. They believe in what Allah sent you with and in what the previous Messengers were sent with; *they do not distinguish between* believing in them, *nor do they reject what they brought from their Lord.* That clause is doing more work than it looks. The temptation of every religious community is to accept the prophet who flatters it and dismiss the one who does not. The verse closes that door from both directions at once.

**Why "before you" is there.**

Maʿārif gives the historical reason, transmitted from ʿAbdullāh ibn Masʿūd and ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿAbbās. In the Prophet's ﷺ lifetime the God-fearing came in two groups. There were those who had been associators and disbelievers and accepted Islam, and there were those who had been among the People of the Book — Jews and Christians — and embraced Islam later. The preceding verse describes the first group. This one describes the second. That is why belief in the earlier Books is mentioned specifically here, and Maʿārif gives the reason it matters: according to the ḥadīth, the second group deserves a double recompense, once for following the earlier Books before the Qurʾān replaced them, and again for following the Qurʾān when it came as the final Book.

**What the double reward requires.**

Maʿārif adds the standing obligation, which is easy to lose in the historical detail. Even today it is obligatory for every Muslim to believe in the earlier Divine Books. Not to follow them — the Qurʾān replaced them — but to believe that they were revealed. A Muslim who doubts that the Torah or the Gospel was ever sent down has a hole in his faith, and the hole is in the same place as the one the hypocrites will be exposed for later in this sūrah. Al-Mukhtaṣar puts the requirement plainly: they believe in what Allah revealed to all the other prophets before you, *without distinction.*

**Sure faith, not merely belief.**

The verse ends on certainty, and the word matters. Al-Jalālayn and Ibn Kathīr both gloss the Hereafter as the Resurrection, the standing, Paradise, the Fire, the reckoning and the Scale. Ibn Kathīr adds the etymology — the Hereafter is so named because it comes after this earthly life — which is a small remark with a large implication. The thing they are certain about is not present. It has not been seen. It is exactly the unseen of the previous verse, now named. So the fourth quality is the third made specific, and *yaqīn* is the quality of belief that survives the absence of evidence.

**The structure Mujāhid noticed.**

Ibn Kathīr preserves a piece of structural criticism that governs the whole opening of the sūrah. Mujāhid said that four verses at the beginning of al-Baqarah describe the believers, two describe the disbelievers, and thirteen describe the hypocrites. Those four verses are the ones you have just read. The Qurʾān has now finished defining the people it is guiding, and from the next verse it turns to the people it is not — two verses of open rejection, and then thirteen of concealed rejection, which is the longer treatment because it is the harder problem.

5.text:
The verdict on the last three verses, and it is emphatic. *It is they who are guided by their Lord, and it is they who will be successful.* The wording shuts the door on everyone else: it is they, and not others, who are guided; it is they, and not others, who succeed. The four qualities just listed were not decoration. They were the test, and these are the people who pass it.

*It is they who are* ˹truly˺ *guided by their Lord, and it is they who will be successful.* The verdict, and it is emphatic in a way the Arabic makes visible. Both clauses are built to restrict: it is they, and no one else, who are guided; it is they, and no one else, who succeed. The four verses have described a kind of person, and this verse says that the description was not decorative. It was a test, and these are the people who pass it.

**Guidance as something given.**

Ibn Kathīr reads *hudā* as light, guidance and insight *from Allah* — the preposition matters, because the guidance is not something the believers generated by being sincere. It arrived. He then ties it back, listing exactly who is being referred to: those who believe in the unseen, establish prayer, spend from what Allah granted them, believe in what was revealed to the Messenger and the Messengers before him, and believe in the Hereafter with certainty — and who prepare for it by doing good and avoiding the prohibitions. Every quality from verses 3 and 4 is recalled, which is how you know this is a verdict on them rather than a new topic.

**Success, defined twice.**

The word is *mufliḥūn*, and the sources gloss it in both directions. Ibn Kathīr: they shall have what they seek and be saved from the evil they tried to avoid — rewards, eternal life in Paradise, safety from the torment prepared for His enemies. Tanwīr al-Miqbās says almost the same thing in different words: they are the ones who shall escape Allah's wrath and torment, and it is also said that these are those who apprehended and found what they were seeking and escaped the evil they were fleeing from. Al-Mukhtaṣar adds the temporal spread: successful in this world and the next. So *falāḥ* is not prosperity and not mere survival. It is getting what you wanted and missing what you feared, in both lives.

**Whom the sources have in mind.**

Tanwīr al-Miqbās ends its gloss by naming the referent — *and these are the Companions of Muḥammad* ﷺ. That is worth noticing, because the verse is not addressed only to them. It is a description that they happened to fulfil first, and the description remains available. Al-Jalālayn keeps it definitional rather than historical: those described in the way mentioned are upon guidance from their Lord, and those are the ones who will succeed in entering Paradise and be saved from the Fire.

**The hinge of the opening.**

This verse is where the first five verses close, and Maʿārif's summary of the whole movement is the clearest statement of what has happened. After affirming the Qurʾān as the Book of Guidance and as beyond all doubt, the first five verses refer to those who derive full benefit from it — the *muʾminūn* or *muttaqūn* — and delineate the qualities that distinguish them from others. The next fifteen verses speak of those who refuse this guidance and oppose it out of spite. So verse 5 is not a summary line. It is a hinge. Everything after it is the counter-case, and it is three times as long.

6.text:
Now the chapter turns to the opposite case, and the turn is abrupt. *As for those who persist in disbelief, it is the same whether you warn them or not.* The verse does not say they refuse the warning. It says the warning makes no difference to them — warned or not warned, the outcome is identical. *They will never believe.* That is a strange thing for a book of guidance to say, and the next verse explains why it is true.

*As for those who persist in disbelief, it is the same whether you warn them or not* — they will never believe. The hinge of verse 5 turns, and the subject changes from people who receive guidance to people who have stopped being able to. Maʿārif sets out the architecture of what follows, and it is the key to the next fifteen verses. There were two distinct groups of those who refused the guidance. One came out in open hostility and rejection, and the Qurʾān calls them *kāfirūn*. The other lacked, through moral depravity and greed, even the courage to say what it thought, and adopted deceit and duplicity instead — convincing the Muslims that it had faith, that it was as good a Muslim as any, and that it would support them. Verse 6 and 7 handle the first group. The thirteen verses after that handle the second, which gets the longer treatment because concealment is the harder thing to diagnose.

**The warning that cannot land.**

The verse's structure is the point. It does not say they reject the warning; it says the warning makes no difference. Al-Jalālayn gives the names the verse was understood to refer to — the likes of Abū Jahl and Abū Lahab — and then explains the word. *Indhār*, warning, is to give knowledge of something and simultaneously instil an element of fear. So a warning has two components, information and alarm, and in these people both channels are closed. Tanwīr al-Miqbās adds the harder reading: they will not believe as it is in Allah's knowledge.

**What "disbelief" means here.**

Ibn Kathīr's gloss is etymological and sharp. *Kafarū* means they covered the truth and hid it. That is not ignorance. It is an act performed on something already known, which is why the warning is useless — you cannot inform a person of something they are already suppressing. He supports it with two parallel cases from the Qurʾān: those against whom the Word of your Lord has been justified will not believe, even if every sign should come to them, until they see the painful torment; and, to the People of the Book, even if you were to bring them all the signs, they would not follow your direction of prayer. Then the pastoral instruction, which is the practical reason the verse exists: *do not pity them — deliver the Message to them.* The Prophet ﷺ is not being told to stop. He is being told not to grieve over the result.

**Why minds close.**

Tazkīrul Qurʾān gives the social mechanism, and it is the most searching thing in these sources about this verse. If one closes one's eyes one will not see; if one blocks one's ears one will not hear; however clear the call of truth may be, it can be understood only if one opens one's mind to it. Then the diagnosis: where society is rigidly bound by age-old conventions, people are less concerned with opening their minds to divine realities than with supporting the vested interests of the existing system. As God's emissary the preacher is neither a representative nor a supporter of those structures, so his call, being new and unfamiliar, *poses itself as a threat to material security.* That is the reason the warning fails. It is not that the argument is weak. It is that accepting it would cost something.

**The two verses as one unit.**

Al-Mukhtaṣar summarizes both at once: those who reject what Allah revealed to His Messenger continue on the wrong path in their stubbornness, so it makes no difference whether you warn them or not. **

**What the Prophet is being spared.**

** There is a mercy in this verse that is easy to miss under its severity. The Prophet ﷺ had spent years warning people who did not change, and the verse tells him in advance that the outcome was never in his hands. Ibn Kathīr's phrase is *deliver the Message to them*, and the instruction that follows is that whoever among them accepts has accepted for his own good. The verse removes the burden of results from the one carrying the message, which is why it is placed before the thirteen verses on hypocrisy rather than after them. Open rejection is survivable for a preacher. It is the concealed kind that makes him doubt whether he was heard at all. The next verse explains the mechanism of that stubbornness, and it is not a metaphor.

7.text:
Here is why the warning fails. *Allah has sealed their hearts and their hearing, and their sight is covered.* Three faculties are named — the heart that judges, the ear that receives instruction, the eye that observes evidence — and all three are shut. This is not a threat about the afterlife. It is a description of something that has already happened to these people, and the tremendous punishment at the end of the verse is where that condition leads.

*Allah has sealed their hearts and their hearing, and their sight is covered. They will suffer a tremendous punishment.* The previous verse said the warning makes no difference; this one says why. And the explanation is uncomfortable, because the sealing is attributed to Allah, not to them. The tradition worked hard on this verse, and Ibn Kathīr preserves the range of what it concluded.

**What "sealed" means.**

As-Suddī gives the plain sense: *khatama Allāh* means Allah has sealed. Qatādah gives the causal sequence, and it is the most important gloss in the verse — Shayṭān controlled them when they obeyed him, and therefore Allah sealed their hearts, hearing and sight, and they could neither see the guidance nor hear, comprehend or understand. The seal is a consequence of an obedience they chose. Mujāhid, via Ibn Jurayj, gives the image: a stamp, which occurs when sin resides in the heart and surrounds it from all sides, and that submersion constitutes the seal. Al-Jalālayn compresses all three — a seal impressed on the hearts so that no good enters them, something deposited in the hearing so that they cannot profit from the truth they hear, and a covering, a veil, on the eyes so that they do not see the truth.

**Three faculties, not one.**

The verse is precise about what is closed, and the precision matters. The heart, the hearing, the sight. Al-Mukhtaṣar draws out each: Allah has sealed their hearts, locking their falsehood inside them; sealed their hearing so they neither listen to nor accept the truth; and put a cover over their eyes so they do not see the truth in its clarity. That is the full apparatus of perception — the organ that judges, the organ that receives instruction, the organ that observes evidence — and the verse says all three are shut. Which is why verse 6 said the warning makes no difference.

**The punishment that is not the Fire.**

Maʿārif makes the argument that gives this verse its real weight. These two verses tell us the other world is where the real punishment for disbelief is received, but some punishment comes in this world too, and it takes a particular form: the divine favour that helps a person reform is withdrawn. Without it, a person keeps growing in disobedience and finally loses even the awareness of evil. Then the maxim that explains the mechanism: one punishment for an evil deed is another evil deed which comes after it, just as one reward for a good deed is another good deed. So the sealing in this verse is not primarily a threat about the afterlife. It is a description of something that has already happened to these people, and the tremendous punishment named at the end of the verse is what that condition leads to.

**Whom it names.**

Tanwīr al-Miqbās identifies the verse with particular people, and offers two sets. It refers to the Jews Kaʿb ibn al-Ashraf, Ḥuyayy ibn Akhṭab and Judayy ibn Akhṭab; or, it is also said, to the idolaters of Makkah — ʿUtbah and Shaybah ibn Rabīʿah and al-Walīd ibn al-Mughīrah. Al-Jalālayn's gloss on the ending is unambiguous about what awaits them: a mighty chastisement, intense and everlasting.

**Where the passage turns.**

Al-Mukhtaṣar marks the transition in a single clause, and it is the cleanest statement of the whole opening's structure. After describing the disbelievers, *who are at fault inside and out*, the Qurʾān now describes the hypocrites, *who appear good on the outside but are not so inwardly.* Thirteen verses follow. Why the sequence matters, Read Qatādah's gloss again and the order is not arbitrary. They obeyed, and therefore Allah sealed. The obedience comes first and the sealing second, which is what keeps the verse from saying that these people were created unable to hear. Ibn Kathīr's own framing of the whole passage makes the same point from the other side: since Allah has written that they would do so, it does not matter whether the Prophet ﷺ warns them or not. Knowledge of what a person will choose is not the cause of his choosing it, and the tradition held both halves of that at once without collapsing either. That is the reason this verse could be read as comfort to the Prophet and as warning to everyone else at the same time. The problem the sūrah is actually working on is not open rejection, which is at least honest, but concealed rejection — and verse 8 introduces it with a sentence that sounds like a confession of faith.

8.text:
A third kind of person appears, and this one is the hardest to spot. *There are some who say, “We believe in Allah and the Last Day,” yet they are not true believers.* What makes this verse devastating is that their sentence is quoted exactly, and the sentence is completely orthodox. Nothing in it is false — except the fact that they are the ones saying it.

*And there are some who say, "We believe in Allah and the Last Day," yet they are not* ˹true˺ *believers.* The thirteenth verse of the sūrah, and the start of the thirteen-verse treatment Mujāhid counted. What makes this verse devastating is not the accusation. It is the quotation. These people are given their own sentence to speak, and the sentence is entirely orthodox. Nothing in it is false except the fact that they are saying it.

**What hypocrisy is.**

Ibn Kathīr defines the term the passage is about. *Nifāq* means to show conformity or agreement and to conceal evil. Then he divides it, and the division is theologically consequential: there is hypocrisy in creed, which causes its people to reside in Hell for eternity, and hypocrisy in deed, which is one of the major sins. Ibn Jurayj's portrait of the hypocrite is the sharpest line in the passage: *his actual deeds are different from what he publicizes, what he conceals is different from what he utters, his entrance and presence are not the same as his exit and absence.* The last clause is the tell. A person who is one thing in front of an audience and another thing on the way out has split himself in two.

**The detail in what they left out.**

Maʿārif notices something in the quotation that only becomes visible when you read it closely, and it is the best observation in these sources on this verse. The hypocrites, with all their hostility to Islam, tried to refrain from lying as far as they could. In claiming to be Muslims they mentioned only their faith in Allah and in the Day of Judgment — and left out faith in the Prophet ﷺ, for fear of telling a lie. Maʿārif draws the conclusion: this shows how disgusting it is to tell a lie. They were prepared to deceive, but not prepared to say the specific sentence that would have been straightforwardly false. So the verse quotes a technically true statement made by people whose whole position is a deception, which is a far more precise indictment than a plain accusation of lying would have been.

**What they claim, and what is missing.**

Tanwīr al-Miqbās unpacks both halves. They say we believe in Allah — in the open, and we are genuine in it — and in the Last Day, believing in resurrection after death whereupon deeds shall be requited. Then the negation: *when they believe not* — neither secretly, nor are they genuine in their belief. Al-Jalālayn adds a grammatical note that carries a theological weight. The plural import of *man*, the singular "whoever" in *man yaqūl*, is taken into account by the plural pronoun *hum* in "they are not believers." The verse uses a singular word and then answers it with a plural, which is how the Qurʾān says that this is a category and not one man.

**The psychology of the position.**

Tazkīrul Qurʾān explains why such people exist at all. For those who put worldly interests and expediency first, total and unconditional devotion to truth appears unwise, because their true allegiance is to those interests and they can only attach themselves to truth superficially. They consider themselves clever. They think they are safeguarding themselves in this world and also qualifying to be considered among the pious. But this is wishful thinking, a figment of imagination rather than a fact of life. Every test removes them further from true religion and closer to their own world-oriented religion, and their hypocrisy is *like a cancer which keeps on growing.* Al-Mukhtaṣar's summary is the plainest: among people are some who claim to have faith in Allah when they actually do not believe. The next verse states what this costs them, and it is not what they think.

9.text:
The verse is one sentence with a reversal in the middle of it. *They seek to deceive Allah and the believers, yet they only deceive themselves.* The target and the victim of the deception trade places. They set out to fool other people. They end up fooling one person. And the last clause is the cruel part: *they fail to perceive it*. They do not even know the deception has failed.

*They seek to deceive Allah and the believers, yet they only deceive themselves, but they fail to perceive it.* The verse is a single sentence with a reversal in the middle of it, and the reversal is the whole point. The object and the subject of the deception trade places. They set out to deceive; they end up deceived; and the final clause says they do not notice.

**The verb and its grammar.**

Al-Jalālayn does the technical work, and it is worth following. The hypocrites deceive God and the believers by manifesting the opposite of the unbelief they hide, so that they can avoid His rulings in this world. Then the reversal: *and only themselves they deceive*, because the evil consequences of their deception rebound on them — they are disgraced in this world when God makes known to His Prophet what they are hiding, and punished in the Hereafter. He adds a linguistic observation that resolves an apparent contradiction. The form *yukhādiʿūn* is a third verbal form, which normally denotes a mutual action, but here it denotes a one-way action, the way *ʿāqabtu al-lissa* — I punished the thief — uses the third form for something done to one party. And the mention of God in the statement is for rhetorical effect.

**Why Allah is named at all.**

Maʿārif takes up exactly that rhetorical effect and makes it the centre of the verse. These verses denounce the hypocrites for trying to be clever with Allah Himself, although no one among them probably had such an intention or even thought of the possibility. What they were actually doing was trying to deceive the Prophet ﷺ and the Muslims. Allah has equated that effort with an attempt to deceive Him, and has thereby indicated that a man who is impertinent to a prophet or a man of Allah is ultimately guilty of impertinence to Allah Himself — and this is true above all of the Prophet ﷺ, who stands at the head of all created beings. So the verse is not saying these people were fools enough to think they could trick God. It is saying that deceiving His Messenger is the same act.

**What they actually deceived.**

Tanwīr al-Miqbās supplies both the manner and the referents. They try to deceive Allah — contravening against Him and denying Him in secret; or, it is said, they were so daring that they thought they had deceived Him. And those who believe: Abū Bakr and all the Companions of Muḥammad ﷺ. Then the reversal stated plainly: they deceive none but themselves, and *they do not know that Allah informs His Prophet about that which lies secret in their hearts.* That is the mechanism of the failure. The deception required the secret to stay secret, and the secret was being reported.

**The one they fooled.**

Al-Mukhtaṣar states the irony in one line: they think they can deceive Allah and the believers by acting outside as if they believe while hiding disbelief inside, but really they only deceive themselves, without realising it — and Allah knows all that is secret and hidden, and has told the believers what these people are like. So the deception did not even achieve its immediate aim. The believers were informed. The only person left being successfully deceived is the deceiver, and verse 10 explains why he cannot see it.

10.text:
The diagnosis of everything since verse 8, given in medical language. *There is sickness in their hearts, and Allah lets their sickness increase.* This is why they could not see their own deception in the last verse — clear sight is one of the things the disease has already taken. And the sickness grows. *They will suffer a painful punishment for their lies.*

*There is sickness in their hearts, and Allah* ˹only˺ *lets their sickness increase. They will suffer a painful punishment for their lies.* The diagnosis of the whole thirteen-verse passage, given in medical language, and it explains verse 9's last clause. They fail to perceive their own deception because perception is one of the things the disease has taken.

**What the disease is.**

Ibn Kathīr preserves the consensus of the early authorities on the word, and it is unusually unanimous. As-Suddī narrated from Abū Mālik and from Abū Ṣāliḥ, from Ibn ʿAbbās, and from Murrah al-Hamadānī from Ibn Masʿūd and other Companions, that *in their hearts is a disease* means doubt, and that *Allah has increased their disease* also means doubt. Mujāhid, ʿIkrimah, al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī, Abū al-ʿĀliyah, ar-Rabīʿ ibn Anas and Qatādah said the same. ʿAbd ar-Raḥmān ibn Zayd ibn Aslam then makes the distinction explicit: a disease in the religion, not a physical disease — they are the hypocrites, and the disease is the doubt they brought with them. Al-Jalālayn names its two components: doubt and hypocrisy, which ail their hearts and debilitate them. Tanwīr al-Miqbās lists four: doubt, hypocrisy, conflict and darkness.

**Why the metaphor is exact.**

Maʿārif gives the definition that makes the image more than decoration. Illness, in the medical sense, is a state in which a person has lost the balanced proportion of the elements within him that keep him healthy, so that his body can no longer function properly, and which may finally lead to his total destruction. In the terminology of the Qurʾān and ḥadīth, the word disease is also applied to mental and psychic states which hinder a person from attaining any degree of spiritual perfection. So the verse is not being poetic. It is claiming that hypocrisy has the structure of an illness — a loss of internal proportion, a failure of function, and a trajectory towards destruction. That is why it explains blindness. A diseased organ does not report accurately.

**The increase.**

The second clause is the frightening one, because the increase is attributed to Allah. Tanwīr al-Miqbās: Allah increased their doubt, hypocrisy, conflict and darkness. Al-Jalālayn gives the instrument, and it is the detail that matters most — *God has increased their sickness with what He has revealed in the Qurʾān, since they disbelieve it.* The revelation is the same revelation that guided the muttaqūn in verse 2. On these people it has the opposite effect, not because it changed but because they did. Al-Mukhtaṣar states the justice of it: because they lied, Allah increases the disease of doubt in their hearts, adding hesitation to their uncertainty, hence they only gain what they deserve.

**The ending and its two readings.**

The verse closes on a painful punishment, and the sources note a genuine textual variant that changes the charge. Al-Jalālayn records it: read *yukadhdhibūn*, implying they used to call the Prophet of God a liar; or *yakdhibūn*, implying their mendacity when saying "we believe." The two readings accuse them of different lies — one about the Prophet, one about themselves — and the verse is left carrying both. Tanwīr al-Miqbās specifies that the torment shall extend to their hearts, which is the disease's own organ, and names the hypocrites the verse refers to: ʿAbdullāh ibn Ubayy, Jadd ibn Qays and Muʿaṭṭib ibn Qushayr.

**Where the passage has arrived.**

Tazkīrul Qurʾān's account of the hypocrites' inner life is the summary of all thirteen verses. Every test in life removes them further from the path of true religion and brings them closer to their own world-oriented religion; their hypocrisy is like a cancer which keeps on growing. That is verse 10 stated as a process rather than a verdict. The sūrah opened with three letters and a claim about a Book. A disease that grows by being fed, The mechanism in this verse is the reverse of ordinary illness, and Maʿārif's definition shows why. A body grows ill when it is deprived of what keeps it in proportion. These hearts grew ill when they were given more of what they had rejected. Every revelation that should have cured them deepened the imbalance instead, because a disease of doubt does not respond to evidence the way a disease of the body responds to medicine. That is the specific terror of the verse. The cure was being administered continuously, in public, in their own language, and it was making them worse. Ten verses later it has drawn three portraits — the guided, the sealed, and the sick — and the third one is still being painted.

11.text:
When these people are told to stop causing trouble, they are genuinely offended. *Do not spread corruption in the land* — and they answer, *We are only peace-makers!* They are not lying about their own opinion of themselves. They really do think they are the ones holding things together. That is what makes the verse uncomfortable. It is not describing a criminal who knows he is a criminal. It is describing someone who cannot see the difference between the two.

**What they are actually told.**

Ibn Kathīr preserves the earliest gloss on what the command means. As-Suddī reports from Ibn ʿAbbās and Ibn Masʿūd that the people addressed are the hypocrites, and that *do not make mischief on the earth* means disbelief and acts of disobedience. So the mischief is not vandalism or violence. It is unbelief, and the acts that follow from it. Al-Jalālayn is more specific about the mechanism: they spread corruption in the land *through unbelief and hindering people from faith.* The damage is done by blocking other people, which is why it is invisible to them.

**Their answer, exactly.**

The Qurʾān quotes them rather than paraphrasing them, and the quotation is short. Al-Jalālayn reads it as a denial with a claim attached: *we are not engaging in corruption* — and positively, we are putting things right. Tanwīr al-Miqbās identifies the addressees as the Jews and glosses the exchange as preventing people from the religion of Muḥammad ﷺ while claiming, *we are reforming it through obedience.* They are not refusing the charge. They are reversing it.

**Why claims settle nothing.**

Maʿārif makes the argument that decides the verse, and it is blunt. Oral claims alone do not decide whether a person is working for order or disorder — *for what thief would call himself a thief?* It depends on what one does, not on what one says. Then the harder half: if a man's activities do result in mischief, he will be called a mischief-maker *even if he had no such intention.* Sincerity is not a defence. The hypocrites may well believe themselves, and it does not change what they are.

**The sophistry named.**

Maʿārif labels these two verses an exposure of the hypocrites' sophistry. Their activities threatened to produce general chaos and disorder, and yet, in their mealy-mouthed way, they pretended to be men of good will serving the cause of peace and order. Al-Mukhtaṣar compresses the whole exchange: when they are told not to ruin things on earth — through their rejection of the truth and their disobedience — they deny doing so, claiming that they only correct things and put them right.

12.text:
One short verse, and it is the answer to the last one. *Indeed, it is they who are the corruptors, but they fail to perceive it.* The Qurʾān does not argue with the hypocrites' claim. It simply contradicts it and then explains why the contradiction will never reach them. They are not resisting a conclusion they have considered. They are incapable of seeing the thing at all.

**The reversal, and its emphasis.**

Al-Jalālayn notes the grammar of the opening. The word *a-lā*, truly, is there for alerting, intended emphatically — so the verse does not merely state the reversal, it flags that something is about to be overturned. *They are the agents of corruption.* The people who called themselves peace-makers are named as the cause of the disorder they claim to be preventing.

**What they cannot see.**

Tanwīr al-Miqbās gives the blindness a direction: they are mischief-mongers by being a hindrance, and they perceive not — *the followers do not know that their leaders mislead them.* So the ignorance is not only at the top. It runs down through the group, and the people being led cannot see that they are being led. Al-Mukhtaṣar states it flatly: it is they who ruin things, but they do not admit this, nor do they know that their actions are the cause of all ruin.

**Why intention does not rescue them.**

Maʿārif's principle from the previous verse applies here in full. A person whose activities result in mischief is a mischief-maker even if he had no such intention. The verse therefore does not accuse the hypocrites of lying about their own motives. It says their motives are irrelevant, and that is a far less comfortable thing to be told.

13.text:
A second exchange, and this one is about intelligence. The hypocrites are told to believe the way other people believe, and they respond with contempt: *Will we believe as the fools believe?* They think faith is for simple people. The verse ends by turning the word back on them — *it is they who are fools, but they do not know* — and the last clause is the point. They do not even know they have been answered.

**Who "others" are.**

Maʿārif settles the reference, and it matters. According to the consensus of commentators, the Arabic word *an-nās*, people, in this verse refers to the Companions of the Prophet ﷺ, because it was just these people who had embraced the faith and accepted the Qurʾān as the word of Allah while it was still being revealed. Al-Jalālayn agrees: believe as the people believe, that is, as the Companions of the Prophet. Tanwīr al-Miqbās narrows it further to ʿAbdullāh ibn Salām and his companions — the Jewish scholars who accepted Islam.

**The standard being set.**

Maʿārif draws the conclusion the tradition took from this, and it is a large one. The verse indicates that the only kind of faith acceptable to Allah is the one similar to that of the Companions, and that the faith of others is worthy of the name only when it resembles theirs. So the command *believe as others believe* is not a call to conform. It is naming a benchmark.

**What they were told to believe.**

Ibn Kathīr unpacks the instruction the hypocrites were sneering at. Believe just as the believers believe in Allah, His angels, His Books, His Messengers, resurrection after death, Paradise and Hellfire — and obey Allah and His Messenger by heeding the commandments and avoiding the prohibitions. That is the whole of it: creed and conduct together. Their reply reduces all of that to stupidity.

**The insult and its target.**

Al-Mukhtaṣar records the tone as well as the words: when they are told to have faith as the Companions did, they reply *looking down on people and making fun of them*, saying should we have faith like simple-minded people do? Al-Jalālayn renders the answer as *shall we believe as fools believe — that is, as the ignorant do? No, we do not follow their way.* Then the refutation: truly they are the foolish ones, but they know this not.

**What "fools" meant to them.**

The insult only works if the word carries a particular weight, and Ibn Kathīr's rendering shows what they thought they were saying. The hypocrites answer *shall we believe as the fools have believed* — and the tradition reads the phrase as a claim about intelligence rather than about doctrine. They are not disputing the content of the faith. They are disputing the calibre of the people who hold it. That is why the refutation is so short. The verse does not defend the Companions. It simply reassigns the adjective.

**The knowledge they lack.**

The closing clause is *but they do not know*, and Al-Jalālayn renders it as *but they know this not* — the thing they do not know is that they are the foolish ones. Maʿārif's reading of the verse as a benchmark makes the ignorance precise: if the only faith acceptable to Allah is the one resembling that of the Companions, then a person who despises that faith has not made a sophisticated choice. He has mistaken the standard for the thing that falls short of it.

14.text:
This verse shows the hypocrites doing the thing, not just claiming it. In front of the believers they say *We believe.* Alone with their own people they say something else entirely: *We are definitely with you; we were only mocking.* Two rooms, two scripts. And the second script reveals what the first was for — the profession of faith was a performance, and its audience was never the believers.

**The two meetings.**

Ibn Kathīr describes the mechanism plainly. When the hypocrites meet the believers, they proclaim their faith and pretend to be believers, loyalists and friends — and they do this to misdirect, mislead and deceive. The motive is not only safety. He adds that they also want a share of the benefits and gains the believers might acquire. Al-Mukhtaṣar makes the same point: they say *we believe what you believe*, as they think it will benefit them to act this way.

**Who their "evil associates" are.**

The verse calls them *shayāṭīn*, devils, and the sources disagree productively about who that means. Al-Jalālayn reads them as their leaders. Tanwīr al-Miqbās names them — soothsayers and leaders, five in number: Kaʿb ibn al-Ashraf in Madīnah, Abū Burdah al-Aslamī in Banū Aslam, Ibn as-Sawdāʾ in al-Shām, ʿAbd ad-Dār in Juhaynah, and ʿAwf ibn ʿĀmir in Banū ʿĀmir. So the second room is not private doubt. It is an organised alternative allegiance.

**The word they chose for faith.**

The second confession is the most damaging thing in the verse. *We were only mocking.* Al-Jalālayn renders it as *we were only mocking them* — the believers — *by feigning belief.* Tanwīr al-Miqbās has them declare to their leaders, *we follow your religion in secret.* So the profession of faith is not described as mistaken or reluctant. It is described as a joke told at someone's expense.

**Where this sits in the chapter.**

Maʿārif places these verses in the architecture of the opening. Sūrat al-Baqarah opens with the declaration that the Qurʾān is beyond all doubt, and its first twenty verses delineate the features of those who believe in it and those who do not: the first five dealing with the God-fearing, the next two with disbelievers who were open and violent in their hostility, and the following thirteen with those crafty disbelievers who claimed to be Muslims but were not. This verse is the thirteenth of that thirteen.

**What the first room was for.**

Ibn Kathīr gives the two motives behind the public profession, and they are different enough to matter. The hypocrites proclaim their faith to misdirect, mislead and deceive the believers — that is protection. But they also want a share of the benefits and gains the believers might possibly acquire — that is profit. So the performance was never only defensive. It was an investment, and the second room is where the investors talk to each other.

**Why the verse quotes both speeches.**

The Qurʾān could have simply said that the hypocrites lie. Instead it reproduces both statements word for word, and the contrast does the work that an accusation could not. In front of the believers the claim is minimal — *we believe.* In front of their own people the claim is total — *we are definitely with you* — and it comes with an explanation of the first speech. The verse lets the two rooms testify against each other. The verse calls the second group *shayāṭīn*, and the sources do not agree on whether that is literal or descriptive. Al-Jalālayn reads them as their leaders, plainly human. Tanwīr al-Miqbās calls them soothsayers and leaders and names five of them across different regions — Madīnah, Banū Aslam, al-Shām, Juhaynah, Banū ʿĀmir. On that reading the word is doing double duty: these are the men the hypocrites actually obeyed, and obeying them is what made the title fit. Maʿārif's count of the opening twenty verses makes this the pivot. Five verses on the God-fearing, two on open disbelievers, thirteen on those who claimed to be Muslims and were not. This verse is the last of the thirteen, and it is the only one that shows the hypocrisy being practised rather than described. Everything before it said what these people were. This one lets them speak. The verse's last word is *mocking*, and the next verse takes it up as the charge against them. Ibn Kathīr's heading for this passage is the hypocrites' cunning and deceit, and his summary of what the two rooms achieved is that they misdirected nobody. The believers were not taken in for long, because the profession was checked against conduct. What the performance did secure was a share of the benefits — and verse 15 states that the payment for it is already being made, in the form of being left exactly as they are.

15.text:
The answer to the mockery, and it is not a punishment yet. *Allah will throw their mockery back at them, leaving them to continue wandering blindly in their defiance.* Nothing happens to them here. No fire, no seizure. They are simply left as they are — and being left is the judgement. The verse says that the worst thing that can happen to a person who is fooling himself is to go on succeeding at it.

**The mockery returned.**

Al-Jalālayn states the exchange exactly: God Himself mocks them, requiting them for their mockery. Al-Mukhtaṣar adds the shape of the repayment — Allah mocks the hypocrites for their mocking of the believers, and He will repay in equal measure. Tanwīr al-Miqbās gives it a scene in the hereafter: He will open a gate of Paradise for them and then shut it before their eyes, and so the believers will mock them. The humiliation they practised is the humiliation they receive.

**What "left to wander" means.**

The second half of the verse is the real sentence. Al-Jalālayn reads it as giving them respite in their insolence — in their transgressing the limits of unbelief — bewildered, wavering in perplexity. Tanwīr al-Miqbās puts it in this world rather than the next: He will leave them in this world blind in their disbelief and error, unable to see either faith or guidance. Al-Mukhtaṣar combines both: they are treated as believers in this world, but will be repaid for their lying and deception in the next, and He allows them to become more and more lost.

**Why they cannot stop.**

Maʿārif explains the complacency the verse is answering. The hypocrites are mightily pleased with themselves in the belief that they can so easily make a fool of the Muslims and get away with it, while they are in fact only making a fool of themselves. The respite is what makes this possible. Because nothing goes wrong for them, they have no evidence that anything is wrong.

**Respite as sentence.**

The verse's two halves are usually read as one promise and one threat, but Al-Jalālayn's gloss makes them the same thing. God mocks them by requiting their mockery, and He leaves them — *giving them respite in their insolence.* The respite is not a delay of punishment. It is the punishment, because it is what allows the insolence to continue.

**The confusion that replaces certainty.**

Al-Jalālayn's last word for their state is *yaʿmahūn* — bewildered, wavering in perplexity. Al-Mukhtaṣar describes the same condition from the other side: He allows them to become more and more lost and to do more and more wrong, so they remain confused and doubtful about the truth. The people who thought they had the clearest view of everyone in the room end up unable to settle anything.

16.text:
A commercial image, and it is the summary of everything since verse 8. *They are the ones who trade guidance for misguidance.* They did not lose their faith or have it taken from them. They exchanged it, deliberately, for something they judged to be worth more. *But this trade is profitless, and they are not guided.* The verse says the deal went through and the buyer got nothing.

**The trade named.**

Ibn Kathīr ties this verse to the parable that follows it: Allah likened the hypocrites, when they bought deviation with guidance and thus acquired utter blindness, to a person who started a fire. The language of buying is the point. Guidance was in their hands — they had heard it, understood it well enough to mock it — and they spent it.

**Why the trade fails.**

The verse does not say the trade was wicked and was therefore cancelled. It says the trade was *profitless*, which is a commercial verdict rather than a moral one. Al-Mukhtaṣar's summary keeps that framing: they are the ones who trade guidance for misguidance, but this trade is profitless, and they are not rightly guided. The buyer is not punished for cheating. He is simply left holding nothing.

**What the loss consists of.**

Maʿārif's reading of the surrounding verses supplies the substance of the loss. The hypocrites are those who claimed to be Muslims but were not, and the consequence is not that they are exposed but that they are left wandering. So the profitless trade costs them the one thing they thought they were securing — safety — and leaves them with the confusion they were trying to avoid.

**What they paid with.**

The verse says they bought misguidance with guidance, which means guidance was the currency. They had it. Ibn Kathīr's account of the surrounding verses makes this concrete — these are people who heard the Qurʾān, understood it well enough to mock it in verse 13, and performed belief in verse 14. Nobody can mock or counterfeit a thing he does not possess. The trade was made from a position of having.

**Why profitless, not sinful.**

The verse chooses commercial language and then refuses to moralise it. It does not say the trade was forbidden or that the buyers will be prosecuted. It says the trade made nothing. Al-Mukhtaṣar keeps that framing in its summary: they trade guidance for misguidance, but this trade is profitless, and they are not rightly guided. The verdict on the transaction is that it failed, which is a stranger and colder thing to be told than that it was wrong.

**The verdict on the transaction.**

Ibn Kathīr ties this verse directly to the parable that follows: Allah likened the hypocrites, when they bought deviation with guidance and thus acquired utter blindness, to a person who started a fire. So the trade is not described and then illustrated. The parable *is* the description of the trade — the fire is what they bought it with, and the darkness is what they received. That is why the next four verses are pictures rather than arguments.

17.text:
Now the Qurʾān stops describing the hypocrites and shows them. *Their example is that of someone who kindles a fire, but when it lights up all around them, Allah takes away their light.* A person in the dark builds a fire. It works. Everything around him becomes visible and he feels safe. Then the light is taken away, and he is left *in complete darkness — unable to see*. The verse is not about a fire. It is about someone who had the truth, used it, and lost it.

**The parable, step by step.**

Ibn Kathīr walks through it. A person starts a fire; when it is lit it illuminates the surrounding area, and the person benefits from it and feels safe. Then the fire is suddenly extinguished, and total darkness covers him. He applies it directly: Allah likened the hypocrites, who bought deviation with guidance and acquired utter blindness, to exactly this.

**What the fire stood for.**

Tanwīr al-Miqbās gives the parable a setting and a meaning. The man lights a fire in the darkness in order to provide safety for his family, his property and his person; when it sheds its light around him he sees what is around him and feels secure — and at that very moment the fire is put out. Then the reading: the hypocrites believed openly in Muḥammad ﷺ and in the Qurʾān, and by doing so they felt their persons, families and properties were safe, avoiding imprisonment or death. The light was real. So was the safety. Both were temporary.

**Two kinds of hypocrite.**

Maʿārif explains why the Qurʾān gives two parables in four verses rather than one. The last four verses bring out the miserable plight of the hypocrites through two extended similes, and the choice of two examples is meant to divide them into two kinds of men. On one side were those in whom disbelief had taken deep roots, who had little inclination towards Islam but pretended to be Muslims for worldly motives — these are the man who found light and lost it again. On the other were those who did recognise the truth of Islam and sometimes wished to be genuine Muslims, but whose worldly interests would not allow it.

**What is taken and when.**

Tanwīr al-Miqbās fixes the moment of loss: *when they die, Allah takes away their light.* So the parable is not about a crisis in this life. The fire burns the whole way through, and it goes out at death. That is the specific horror of the image — the safety was genuine for as long as it lasted, which is exactly why they never questioned it.

**Why a fire and not a lamp.**

Tanwīr al-Miqbās's setting explains the choice of image. The man lights a fire in the darkness in order to provide safety for his family, his property and his person. A fire is not decoration and it is not comfort — it is what a traveller in open country uses to keep predators and thieves away. That is why its going out is catastrophic rather than merely inconvenient. The hypocrites' profession of faith was the same kind of thing: protection, and nothing more.

**The moment the light goes.**

The verse says the fire lit up all around him, and then Allah took the light away. Tanwīr al-Miqbās fixes the timing as death — the hypocrites believed openly and felt their persons, families and properties were safe, avoiding imprisonment or death, and *when they die* Allah takes away their light. So the parable is not about a crisis during life. The fire burns the entire way through, which is exactly why the man never thinks to question it. Maʿārif's reading of the pair gives verse 17 its place. The first simile covers those in whom disbelief had taken deep roots, who had little inclination towards Islam but pretended to be Muslims for worldly motives — the man who found light and lost it again. The second, beginning in verse 19, covers those who did recognise the truth and sometimes wished to be genuine Muslims but whose worldly interests would not allow it. The first group never wanted the light. The second wanted it and could not keep it. Ibn Kathīr's wording on the moment of loss is worth keeping: when the fire was lit and illuminated the surrounding area, the person benefited from it and felt safe — *then the fire was suddenly extinguished*, and total darkness covered him. The word is suddenly. There was no warning and no decline. The safety was complete right up until the moment it was not, which is the specific thing the parable is saying about a faith held only for what it provides.

18.text:
Three words, and they close the first parable. *They are deaf, dumb, and blind, so they will never return.* Each of the three is a sense that has stopped working, and together they cover everything by which a person could get back: hearing the way, asking the way, seeing the way. The last clause is the sentence — *they will never return* — and it does not say they will not be allowed to. It says they will not.

**Each sense, separately.**

Al-Jalālayn takes the three in order. Deaf to the truth, so that they cannot hear it and accept it. Dumb, mute as regards goodness, unable to speak of it. Blind to the path of guidance, so that they cannot perceive it. And then: they shall not return from error. Al-Mukhtaṣar compresses the same three — unable to hear and accept the truth or speak about it, and blind to seeing the truth, so they do not turn back from their error.

**Pretending, not being.**

Tanwīr al-Miqbās offers a sharper reading of the three adjectives: *deaf* — pretending to be deaf; *dumb* — pretending to be dumb; *blind* — pretending to be blind; so they return not from their disbelief and error. On this reading the verse is not describing a disability that happened to them. It is describing a performance they chose, which is consistent with the mockery of verse 14.

**Why the parable ends here.**

Maʿārif places verse 18 as the close of the first simile. The man who kindled a fire and lost its light is the hypocrite in whom disbelief had taken deep roots, who pretended to be Muslim for worldly motives. The three senses name what he has lost by the end of it — and the second parable, beginning in the next verse, describes a different kind of person entirely.

19.text:
A second picture, and it is much more violent. Instead of a fire going out, this is a storm. *A rainstorm from the sky with darkness, thunder, and lightning.* People caught in it press their fingers into their ears at every thunderclap, *for fear of death*. The verse ends by saying that Allah surrounds them — there is nowhere in this scene to step out of.

**The word for the storm.**

Al-Jalālayn does the linguistic work. The likeness of them is as a cloudburst — *ka-ṣayyib*, a term originally *ṣayyūb*, from the verb *ṣāba yasūbu*, meaning it came down — out of the heaven, that is, out of the clouds. In those clouds is darkness layer upon layer, and thunder, and lightning.

**What each part of the storm is.**

Tanwīr al-Miqbās reads the whole scene as the Qurʾān itself. The likeness of the hypocrites and the Jews in relation to the Qurʾān is like rain poured down from heaven at night onto the wilderness — and such is the Qurʾān. It has come down from Allah. It contains darkness, as embodied in the exposition of seditions; thunderings of rebuke whereby fear is instilled; and lightning of exposition, instruction and promise. Al-Mukhtaṣar gives the same mapping: the rain is the Qurʾān, the thunderclap its warnings, and the lightning the truths that appear to them from time to time.

**What thunder and lightning are made of.**

Al-Jalālayn preserves a striking gloss on the middle term. The thunder is the angel in charge of the clouds — it is also said that the thunder is actually the sound of his voice — and the lightning is the flash caused by his voice, which he uses to drive them. So the two things the travellers are reacting to have a single source, and it is not weather.

**The gesture of fear.**

The people in the storm put their fingers — al-Jalālayn specifies their fingertips — in their ears against the thunderclaps, the violent sound, for fear of death. Tanwīr al-Miqbās reads the gesture: they thrust their fingers in their ears by reason of the thunderclaps, for fear of death. Al-Mukhtaṣar names what the gesture means: covering their ears against the thunderclaps is their turning away from the truth and not responding to it.

**The verse's last word.**

Ibn Kathīr's rendering keeps the closing clause attached to the scene: they thrust their fingers in their ears to keep out the stunning thunderclap for fear of death — *but Allah ever encompasses the disbelievers.* The fear of death drives them to block their ears, and the verse answers that there is no direction to run in.

**Night, and open country.**

Tanwīr al-Miqbās's setting for the second parable is more specific than the verse itself, and it changes the picture. The rain is poured down from heaven *at night onto the wilderness.* So the travellers are not merely caught in bad weather. They are in open country, in the dark, with no shelter and no route — which is why the thunder is a matter of life and death rather than discomfort. Al-Mukhtaṣar's mapping is the clearest statement of what the parable is doing. The rain in the storm is the Qurʾān; the thunderclap is its warnings; the lightning is the truths appearing to them from time to time. So the thing the travellers are cowering from is not hostile to them. It is the revelation, and the parts of it that frighten them are the parts that are true. The gesture is the whole verse. Al-Jalālayn specifies that they put their fingertips in their ears against the thunderclaps, the violent sound, for fear of death. Al-Mukhtaṣar names what that means: covering their ears against the thunderclaps is their turning away from the truth and not responding to it. The fear is not of the storm. It is of what the storm is saying. Ibn Kathīr keeps the closing clause attached to the picture: they thrust their fingers in their ears to keep out the stunning thunderclap for fear of death — *but Allah ever encompasses the disbelievers.* The verse ends by removing the possibility the gesture assumes. Plugging your ears only makes sense if you can leave. The last clause says they cannot. Al-Jalālayn's derivation of the word for the storm gives the rain a direction: *ka-ṣayyib*, originally *ṣayyūb*, from *ṣāba yasūbu*, it came down. The term is built from descent rather than from water, which fits Tanwīr al-Miqbās's reading that the rain is the Qurʾān coming down from Allah. So the storm is not weather that happens to the travellers. It is something sent, and it contains darkness in the exposition of seditions, thunderings of rebuke whereby fear is instilled, and lightning of exposition, instruction and promise — all three at once.

20.text:
The storm continues, and the verse follows the travellers through it. *It is as if the lightning were about to snatch away their sight. Whenever lightning strikes, they walk in its light, but when darkness covers them, they stand still.* They are not lost. They are moving — but only in flashes, and only when the light is given to them. The chapter's twenty-verse opening ends on that image, and on the note that Allah could have taken their hearing and sight entirely.

**The walking and the stopping.**

Al-Jalālayn gives the movement its meaning. The lightning almost snatches away their sight — it takes it away swiftly; whenever it gives them light they walk in it, and when the darkness is over them they stop, that is, they stand still. Then the interpretation: it is a simile of the perturbation that the Qurʾānic arguments cause in their hearts, and of their acknowledging the truths of what they love to hear and recoiling from what they detest.

**What the flashes correspond to.**

Tanwīr al-Miqbās maps the movement onto the hypocrites' actual behaviour, and it is the most concrete reading in these sources. When the hypocrites declared themselves to be believers, they went along with what the believers went along with, because their outward faith was accepted. But when they died, they remained in the darkness of the grave. So the walking is the profession of faith, and the standing still is what follows it.

**The reading that makes it a mercy.**

Al-Mukhtaṣar offers the most sympathetic line available on this verse. The brightness of the lightning almost blinds them; whenever it flashes they go forward, and when there is no light they remain in darkness, unable to move. Then: the lightning is the truths appearing to them from time to time. On this reading the flashes are not taunts. They are genuine moments of clarity, and the tragedy is that the travellers only move during them.

**The closing claim.**

The verse ends on power rather than on the travellers. Al-Jalālayn: had God willed, He would have taken away their hearing and their sight — the exterior faculty, in the same way that He took away their inner one. Truly God has power over all things that He wills. Ibn Kathīr's rendering agrees: if Allah willed, He could have taken away their hearing and their sight; certainly, Allah has power over all things. The storm is not the worst thing that could have happened to them.

**Where the twenty verses end.**

Maʿārif's summary of this block closes the opening of the sūrah. The last four verses bring out the miserable plight of the hypocrites through two extended similes, dividing them into two kinds: those in whom disbelief had taken deep roots and who pretended to be Muslim for worldly motives, and those who recognised the truth and sometimes wished to be genuine Muslims but whose worldly interests would not allow it. Twenty verses in, the Qurʾān has drawn three portraits — the guided, the sealed, and the sick — and the third has been given thirteen verses and two parables.

**Light that almost destroys.**

The verse opens on a strange note: the lightning *almost* snatches away their sight. It does not. Al-Jalālayn reads the word as taking it away swiftly, and the near-miss is the point — the same light that lets them see is close to blinding them. Tanwīr al-Miqbās applies it: the exposition of the Qurʾān almost snatched away their error. The clarity is uncomfortable precisely because it works. The travellers walk when it flashes and stand still when it darkens, and Al-Jalālayn gives the pattern its meaning: it is a simile of the perturbation the Qurʾānic arguments cause in their hearts, and of their acknowledging the truths of what they love to hear and recoiling from what they detest. So the movement is real and it is not progress. They cover ground only in the moments when the revelation says something they approve of. Al-Mukhtaṣar's reading of the lightning is the one that keeps this verse from being purely a condemnation. The lightning is the truths appearing to them from time to time. On that reading the flashes are not taunts but genuine moments of clarity, offered repeatedly — and the tragedy is not that the travellers are denied light, but that they only move while it lasts. Maʿārif's summary of this block closes the opening of the sūrah. The last four verses bring out the miserable plight of the hypocrites through two extended similes, dividing them into those in whom disbelief had taken deep roots and pretended to be Muslim for worldly motives, and those who recognised the truth and sometimes wished to be genuine Muslims but whose worldly interests would not allow it. Twenty verses in, three portraits have been drawn, and the third has taken thirteen verses and two parables.
